JEDI: Joint Embedding Diffusion World Model for Online Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

Jing Yu Lim    Rushi Shah    Zarif Ikram    Samson Yu    Haozhe Ma    Tze-Yun Leong    Dianbo Liu Affiliation: National University of Singapore Affiliation: {jing.yu, shah.15, leongty, dianbo}@nus.edu.sg, zikram@usc.edu, Affiliation: {samson.yu, haozhe.ma}@u.nus.edu.sg
Abstract

Diffusion world models have recently become competitive for online model-based reinforcement learning, but current approaches expose a tension: pixel diffusion is effective but computationally expensive while the latest latent diffusion approach improves efficiency yet performs subpar. The latter also relies on separately trained latents rather than the end-to-end world-model objectives that have driven much of modern MBRL progress. In particular, JEPA-style predictive representation learning has emerged as an especially promising direction for world modeling and MBRL. Concurrently, diffusion-style objectives have gained traction across multiple domains, with iterative refinement as a promising approach for multimodal and stochastic targets. Taken together, these trends motivate Joint Embedding DIffusion (JEDI), the first online end-to-end latent diffusion world model. JEDI learns its latent space directly from the diffusion denoising loss with a JEPA framework, using denoising to learn and predict future latents rather than relying on reconstruction and pretrained models. We provide a theoretical motivation showing that conventional JEPA objectives induce a predictive information bottleneck, and that conditional diffusion denoising admits a closely related predictive-compression decomposition. Empirically, JEDI is competitive on Atari100k and outperforms the baseline with seperately trained latents where directly comparable. Relative to the pixel diffusion baseline, JEDI uses 43% less VRAM, over 3×\times faster world-model sampling, and 2.5×\times faster training. JEDI also exhibits a markedly different task-level performance profile from the pixel baseline, suggesting that end-to-end predictive latents change more than compute alone.

1 Introduction

Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) uses a learned world model [59, 23] to predict future outcomes and improve sample efficiency for training an online RL agent [24]. Diffusion models have recently emerged as a powerful backbone for world modeling, especially in visually complex domains [37, 46, 10]. However, the strongest online diffusion world models for MBRL, DIAMOND, still operate in pixel space, where denoising is expensive in memory, sampling time, and training time [3]. A natural next step is therefore to move diffusion into latent space.

Recent latent diffusion approaches such as Horizon Imagination (HI) [16] show that this can improve efficiency, but they learn their latents without end-to-end sequential prediction and do not yet match the performance of DIAMOND [3]. This leaves a clear opportunity: if much of the past progress in MBRL has come from end-to-end representation learning with world-model objectives, then latent diffusion may benefit from the same principle [25, 24, 26, 27, 73, 49].

One especially promising way to instantiate the principle of end-to-end predictive representation learning is through Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA). The goal is to learn representations that capture the predictable, abstract structure of the world while avoiding the need to reconstruct every low-level or intrinsically unpredictable detail [52, 22, 35, 4, 8]. That inductive bias is especially appealing for MBRL, where the latent should retain information useful for future prediction, rewards, and control, while discarding nuisance variation that is irrelevant for decision making [29, 28, 5, 65, 41].

In parallel, there has been a general shift toward diffusion-style objectives rather than one-shot prediction across several domains. These include policy learning [15, 66, 21], language modeling [38, 48, 36], and even classification [9]. These works suggest that diffusion is especially useful for multimodal, stochastic, or sequential targets, where iterative denoising can support more expressive prediction and greater robustness to uncertainty. In the context of MBRL, this makes diffusion a relevant objective to examine for end-to-end latent world models.

Taken together, these observations raise a natural question: can a diffusion world model learn its latent representation end to end from the denoising objective with JEPA? We answer yes. We introduce Joint Embedding DIffusion (JEDI), a latent diffusion world model that trains its encoder end-to-end through conditional denoising, together with reward and end prediction (fig. 1). To our knowledge, JEDI is the first online end-to-end latent diffusion world model built on a JEPA framework.

We show that this representation-learning strategy is theoretically motivated (section 2): latent conditional diffusion admits a variational information-bottleneck decomposition [2, 61, 56], helping explain why latent conditional denoising can support end-to-end latent learning in a world model.

Empirically, JEDI delivers strong results on full Atari100k [33] and in supporting Craftium [42] experiments (figs. 4, 6 and 5) while dramatically improving efficiency over DIAMOND (figs. 8 and 1), using 43% less VRAM, more than 3×\times faster world-model sampling, and more than 2.5×\times faster training.

More broadly, these results suggest that predictive latent diffusion is a promising alternative to latents trained separately with reconstruction and perceptual losses for online MBRL. While DIAMOND remains a strong baseline, our results suggest that end-to-end predictive latents may offer a more attractive path forward when both efficiency and performance matter. Finally, we also observe a markedly different performance profile across games relative to DIAMOND (figs. 11 and 15), suggesting that end-to-end predictive latents change more than compute alone (section 5).

2 Theoretical Motivation: Information Bottleneck in JEPA

We show that JEPA can be given a variational information-bottleneck interpretation [56, 61, 2] complementary to prior formulations for self-supervised representation learning [64, 54]. With the Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM) in fig. 2, the bottleneck structure emerges directly from the JEPA predictive objective:

ℒJEPA:=𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)​qϕ​(z1∣x1)[DKL(qϕ(z2∣x2)∥pθ(z2∣z1))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})q_{\phi}(z_{1}\mid x_{1})}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(q_{\phi}(z_{2}\mid x_{2})\,\|\,p_{\theta}(z_{2}\mid z_{1})\bigr)\right]. (1)

Here, x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} can denote sequential observations in an MDP, with the action omitted for clarity, or two views in a multiview SSL setting. In practice, this KL reduces to cross-entropy for categorical targets and to mean-squared error for fixed-variance Gaussian targets, corresponding to existing works [13, 4]. This KL term is also common in canonical end-to-end MBRL works [24, 26, 27, 29, 28]. Appendix A makes this precise and shows that the JEPA objective can be written as

−ℒJEPA=I⁡(X1,X2)−I^​(X1,Z1)−I^​(X2,Z2)+ℛ1−𝒢,-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}=I(X_{1};X_{2})-\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1})-\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2})+\mathcal{R}_{1}-\mathcal{G}, (2)

where I^​(Xi,Zi)\widehat{I}(X_{i};Z_{i}) are variational mutual-information estimates, ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} is the bottleneck regularizer, and 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the posterior approximation gap. Using the data processing inequality yields the bound:

−ℒJEPA≤I⁡(Z1,Z2)−I^​(X1,Z1)−I^​(X2,Z2)+ℛ1−𝒢.-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}\leq I(Z_{1};Z_{2})-\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1})-\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2})+\mathcal{R}_{1}-\mathcal{G}. (3)

The decomposition makes an information-bottleneck structure explicit. More precisely, it shows that the predictive JEPA loss appears inside a variational bottleneck objective (recovering that full objective would additionally require explicit optimization of ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}). Nonetheless, if we treat Z2Z_{2} as the target label and Z1Z_{1} as the learned representation, then the JEPA objective mirrors the deep variational information bottleneck [2]: it rewards representations that retain information useful for predicting the target through the I⁡(Z1,Z2)I(Z_{1};Z_{2}) term, while penalizing information retained about the inputs through the compression terms. In our setting, this compression naturally appears symmetrically across the two input branches, through I^​(X1,Z1)\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1}) and I^​(X2,Z2)\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2}).

2.1 Information Bottleneck in JEDIś Latent Conditional Diffusion

The same perspective extends to latent conditional diffusion. This connection is especially natural from the PGM perspective underlying DDPM [30], extended to the latent space (fig. 3). In JEDI, one-step latent prediction is replaced by a latent conditional denoising process that predicts the clean future latent (z20z_{2}^{0}) while conditioning on the current latent (z10z_{1}^{0}) and noised future latent (z2tz_{2}^{t}). Following standard DDPM training, we optimize a conditional denoising objective consisting of an endpoint loss term ℒ0\mathcal{L}^{0} and denoising KLs:

ℒCDJden\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{den}} :=ℒ0+𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)​∑t=2T𝔼qφ​(z10∣x1)​qφ​(z20∣x2)​q​(z2t∣z20)​DKL​(q⁡(z2t−1∣z2t,z20)∥pψ​(z2t−1∣z2t,z10))\displaystyle:=\mathcal{L}^{0}+\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\varphi}(z_{1}^{0}\mid x_{1})q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})q(z_{2}^{t}\mid z_{2}^{0})}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{2}^{0})\,\middle\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})\right) (4)

where the loss is typically implemented as regressing towards sampled noise [30]. This yields an analogous information-bottleneck structure (Appendix A.2):

−ℒCDJden≤I⁡(Z10,Z20)−I^​(X1,Z10)−I^​(X2,Z20)+ℛ1+ℛ2,T−𝒢+𝒞2,-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{den}}\leq I(Z_{1}^{0};Z_{2}^{0})-\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1}^{0})-\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2}^{0})+\mathcal{R}_{1}+\mathcal{R}_{2,T}-\mathcal{G}+\mathcal{C}_{2}, (5)

where ℛ2,T\mathcal{R}_{2,T} is the terminal prior-matching term, and 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} is a constant with deterministic encoders. In our current implementation, we optimize this denoising term rather than the full objective augmented with ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}. This perspective also points to a natural extension: explicitly regularizing the bottleneck term, potentially in ways related to recent collapse-prevention methods such as VICReg and LeJEPA [55, 6] (sections A.2.1 and A.2.1).

This is the central mathematical motivation for JEDI: latent conditional denoising is not merely a generative surrogate, but supplies the predictive term in a JEPA-style variational bottleneck decomposition. Accordingly, our claim is that diffusion denoising provides a principled end-to-end predictive learning signal for the latent encoder, rather than that the method exactly optimizes the complete variational objective.

3 Method

3.1 JEDI: Joint Embedding DIffusion World Model

We introduce the Joint Embedding DIffusion World Model (JEDI), which learns an end-to-end latent space encoder while leveraging a diffusion dynamics model. The encoder compresses the observation into a clean latent zt0z_{t}^{0}, the dynamics model predicts the next latent through conditional denoising, and reward and termination are predicted from the latent state. The world model is

World Model:{Encoder:zt0=𝐄ϕ​(xt),Latent diffusion dynamics:z^t+10∼𝐒⁡(𝐃θ​(z^t+1τ,Ztτ)),Reward and termination:(r^t,d^t)=𝐑ψ​(zt0),\textbf{World Model:}\begin{cases}\text{Encoder:}&z_{t}^{0}=\mathbf{E}_{\phi}(x_{t}),\\ \text{Latent diffusion dynamics:}&\hat{z}_{t+1}^{0}\sim\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{D}_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+1}^{\tau},Z_{t}^{\tau})),\\ \text{Reward and termination:}&(\hat{r}_{t},\hat{d}_{t})=\mathbf{R}_{\psi}(z_{t}^{0}),\end{cases} (6)

where tt is the environment time step, xt∈[0,1]64×64×3x_{t}\in[0,1]^{64\times 64\times 3} is the observation, zt0∈[−3,3]16×8×8z_{t}^{0}\in[-3,3]^{16\times 8\times 8} is the clean latent, and τ\tau is the diffusion time step sampled from a log-normal distribution that determines the noise scale. We write Ztτ:=(cnoiseτ,zt−3:t0,at−3:t)Z_{t}^{\tau}:=(c_{\mathrm{noise}}^{\tau},z^{0}_{t-3:t},a_{t-3:t}) for the conditioning tuple consisting of the diffusion-time embedding, past latent states, and past actions. As in EDM [34], we use the preconditioned denoiser

𝐃θ​(zt+1τ,Ztτ)=cskipτ​zt+1τ+coutτ​𝐅θ​(cinτ​zt+1τ,Ztτ).\mathbf{D}_{\theta}(z_{t+1}^{\tau},Z_{t}^{\tau})=c_{\mathrm{skip}}^{\tau}z_{t+1}^{\tau}+c_{\mathrm{out}}^{\tau}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}\bigl(c_{\mathrm{in}}^{\tau}z_{t+1}^{\tau},Z_{t}^{\tau}\bigr). (7)

Here cnoiseτc_{\mathrm{noise}}^{\tau} is a fixed transformation of τ\tau, while cskipτc_{\mathrm{skip}}^{\tau}, coutτc_{\mathrm{out}}^{\tau}, and cinτc_{\mathrm{in}}^{\tau} are the standard EDM preconditioning coefficients that improve the behavior of the neural network 𝐅θ\mathbf{F}_{\theta}. Training and inference follow the same conditioning pipeline shown in fig. 1. During training, the encoder first derives zt−3:t+10z_{t-3:t+1}^{0} from observations xt−3:t+1x_{t-3:t+1}. The future latent zt+1τz_{t+1}^{\tau} is then obtained by perturbing zt+10z_{t+1}^{0} with diffusion noise at level τ\tau, and 𝐅θ\mathbf{F}_{\theta} is trained to predict the direction toward the clean next latent. During inference, the conditioning tuple is formed in the same way, except that the future latent is initialized from noise and the solver 𝐒\mathbf{S} iteratively denoises it to obtain z^t+10\hat{z}_{t+1}^{0}.

The key training signal is the joint embedding diffusion loss

𝔼z1:T∼q,x1:T∼p,τ∼LN[‖∑t=1T𝐅θ(cinτsg(zt+1τ),Ztτ)−1coutτ(sg(zt+10)−cskipτsg(zt+1τ))‖2].\begin{split}\mathbb{E}_{z_{1:T}\sim q,x_{1:T}\sim p,\tau\sim\textnormal{LN}}\Bigg[\left\|\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}\bigl(c_{\mathrm{in}}^{\tau}\mathrm{sg}(z_{t+1}^{\tau}),Z_{t}^{\tau}\bigr)-\frac{1}{c_{\mathrm{out}}^{\tau}}\bigl(\mathrm{sg}(z_{t+1}^{0})-c_{\mathrm{skip}}^{\tau}\,\mathrm{sg}(z_{t+1}^{\tau})\bigr)\right\|^{2}\Bigg].\end{split} (8)

where q⁡(zt)q(z_{t}) denotes the deterministic pushforward of the observation distribution through the encoder, and sg\mathrm{sg} denotes stop-gradient. The reward and termination head is trained with

𝔼z1:T0∼q,(x1:T,r1:T,d1:T)∼p∑t=1TCE(𝐑ψ(zt0),(rt,dt)).\begin{split}\mathbb{E}_{z_{1:T}^{0}\sim q,(x_{1:T},r_{1:T},d_{1:T})\sim p}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\textnormal{CE}(\mathbf{R_{\psi}}(z_{t}^{0}),(r_{t},d_{t})).\end{split} (9)

Crucially, gradients from both losses update the encoder directly through zt0z_{t}^{0}, so the latent is learned through predictive world-model training rather than through reconstruction.

3.2 Practical Design Choices

Several design choices are important in practice. First, to reduce representation collapse, we apply stop-gradient to the future latent target and set the encoder learning rate to 0.3 times the denoiser learning rate, following the spirit of JEPA and TDMPC2 [4, 28]. This allows the encoder to learn directly from the denoising objective while preventing unstable feedback through the future latent target. Second, to stabilize iterative denoising in latent space, we clamp latent activations with the differentiable transform C⁡(z)=tanh⁡(z/s)​sC(z)=\tanh(z/s)s with s=3s=3, applied to both encoder outputs and denoiser outputs. This is common practice: DIAMOND clamps pixels to the natural [−1,1][-1,1] image range and discretizes that range into 256 bins, while HI uses a plain tanh\tanh to clamp latents [3, 16]. Third, with every trajectory batch we randomly switch with uniform probability between using the denoiser output 𝐃θ\mathbf{D}_{\theta} and the encoder output 𝐄ϕ\mathbf{E}_{\phi} as the next-step conditioning signal. This balances near-horizon consistency with sufficient direct encoder supervision.

The policy is trained in an actor-critic framework [26, 3]. We intentionally use REINFORCE [67] so that the actor does not require backpropagation through multi-step denoising, which keeps policy learning lightweight despite the iterative diffusion world model.

4 Experiments

Experimental Setup

Our primary baselines are DIAMOND [3] and HI [16]. DIAMOND is the canonical online pixel-space diffusion world model and the cleanest comparison for the central pixel-versus-end-to-end-latent question. HI is the most relevant latent-diffusion comparison, since it shows that latent diffusion can be efficient but does not learn the latent space end to end through the predictive world-model objective. We also compare against DreamerV3, STORM11 1 We derive the latest updated STORM results from [72], TWM, IRIS, and TWISTER when published numbers are available [27, 73, 72, 49, 43, 12].

We evaluate JEDI primarily on the full Atari100k benchmark with 26 tasks and 5 seeds per task [33]. Each run takes about two days on an A100. For each task, we report the better result from two diffusion-model batch sizes, 32 and 64. Following Agarwal et al. [1], we emphasize interquartile mean, optimality gap, performance profile of the Human-Normalized Scores (HNS), and we use bootstrap sampling for error bars when seed-level data are available. Refer to section B.1 for more details.

In addition to Atari100k, we evaluate on Craftium [42], a 3D embodied Minecraft-like decision-making environment that lets us test whether JEDI transfers beyond 2D Atari. For Craftium, we run 3 seeds per task. Craftium also gives the clearest direct empirical comparison to HI, since it reports published training-curve results there but not on the full Atari100k benchmark.

Har-HNS

Arithmetic mean HNS is an important aggregate metric, but it is disproportionately influenced by already high-valued games and can therefore obscure large relative gains on low-HNS tasks [20, 14]. As a result, methods that improve low-HNS games can appear less impressive under arithmetic averaging than their task-level profile would suggest. Critically, although JEDI and DIAMOND have similar mean HNS, they improve in very different HNS regimes (figs. 11 and 15).

Inspired by the F1 score [63], the use of harmonic mean provides a complementary perspective by emphasizing improvements where performance is still poor. Formally, we define

Har​-​HNS=(1N​∑i=1N1HNSi+0.1)−1,\mathrm{Har\text{-}HNS}=\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\mathrm{HNS}_{i}+0.1}\right)^{-1}, (10)

where NN is the number of games, HNSi\mathrm{HNS}_{i} is the average HNS for game ii, and the offset of 0.10.1 ensures numerical stability for negative HNS values. Intuitively, mean HNS asks how much total score we collect across tasks, whereas Har-HNS asks how well we are doing on the tasks that remain very difficult. We therefore use Har-HNS as a complement to mean HNS to better understand the changed performance profile induced by end-to-end latent diffusion.

4.1 Main Atari100k Results

As shown in fig. 4 and the full per-game breakdown in Appendix table 5, JEDI achieves strong Atari100k performance. It matches or exceeds strong baselines on IQM, optimality gap, and number of state-of-the-art game scores, while remaining competitive on arithmetic mean HNS and achieving runner-up performance in the number of superhuman tasks.

On the four Atari tasks reported by HI, JEDI also performs better overall on the shared subset (fig. 6). This sharpens the paper’s main empirical point. The contribution is not merely that latent diffusion can be cheaper than pixel diffusion, but that an end-to-end predictive denoising, trained directly through the world-model objective, is sufficient to support a competitive online diffusion world model without the need for a pretrained model for learning latents.

Stochastic Atari.

All of Atari100k tasks are deterministic. To test whether diffusion helps model stochastic targets, we compare JEDI with DreamerV3, an MLP-based end-to-end latent world model, on three Atari environments with random frameskips between 2 and 6. JEDI consistently outperforms DreamerV3, suggesting that diffusion may be more robust to high task-related aleatoric uncertainty.

4.2 Craftium Results

Craftium provides supporting evidence that JEDI is not specific to Atari100k. As shown in fig. 5, the same qualitative picture appears here as well: end-to-end predictive latents can support a strong latent diffusion world model without reconstruction-based latent training. In a direct comparison with HI on four Craftium tasks, JEDI performs better overall. Because Craftium is a 3D embodied Minecraft-like environment, these results also suggest that the approach extends beyond 2D Atari.

4.3 Efficiency and Scalability

As summarized in fig. 8, relative to DIAMOND, JEDI uses 43% less VRAM, achieves more than 3×\times faster world-model sampling, and trains more than 2×\times faster. These gains come from moving diffusion from an observation in ℝ64×64×3\mathbb{R}^{64\times 64\times 3} to a 12×\times smaller zt0∈ℝ16×8×8z_{t}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{16\times 8\times 8} compact learned latent with end-to-end training. This is the clearest practical takeaway of the paper: predictive latent diffusion is much more scalable than pixel-space diffusion for online MBRL.

The most relevant efficiency comparison is DIAMOND: as shown in table 1, JEDI stays competitive while cutting A100 training time from 98 to 38 hours at the same parameter count. HI is faster, but JEDI better preserves latent diffusion’s efficiency advantage without giving up competitive end-to-end performance.

4.4 Ablation Study

We conduct two sets of ablation studies, each over five Atari tasks. The first set studies how the latent representation is learned, while the second isolates several stabilization and design choices.

Latent Learning ablation

Figure 9 shows that how the latent space is learned matters. Full JEDI performs best. Replacing the denoising objective with direct next-state MSE prediction reduces performance, and removing diffusion-loss gradients hurts further. Using a separately trained VAE latent performs worst, while adding decoder gradients also slightly hurts performance.

Overall, these ablations support learning the latent space jointly with the predictive world model and point to the denoising objective as a key training signal.

Design Choice Ablation

We also study the design choices that help make end-to-end latent diffusion stable and competitive (fig. 10). Variants using an EMA target encoder, deterministic switching, or no random switching perform worse than the default design, and removing switching together with latent clamping hurts further. Still, HNS remains high across these ablations, suggesting that these design choices are helpful rather than critical. The end-to-end predictive objective appears to be the main ingredient, while the stabilization techniques remain important supporting details.

5 Discussion

5.1 Performance Profile and Har-HNS

JEDI has a distinctly different performance profile from DIAMOND (fig. 11). Importantly, we build directly on top of DIAMOND and keep the experimental setup as close as possible, with the main change being the end-to-end JEPA latent space and only minor hyperparameter adjustments (appendix B). JEDI’s top quantile of relative gains occurs where DIAMOND’s HNS is very low (mean ≈0.06\approx 0.06), whereas DIAMOND’s top quantile occurs in much higher-HNS regimes (mean ≈0.81\approx 0.81), as shown in figs. 11 and 15.

This accounts for fig. 4 the aggregate ranking flips under Har-HNS (section 4): although JEDI (1.4501.450) is slightly below DIAMOND (1.4591.459) on arithmetic mean HNS (table 5), it attains the strongest Har-HNS at 0.3770.377, ahead of DIAMOND (0.3190.319). This indicates that JEDI fails less severely on the games that remain hardest.

5.2 Why Does the Performance Profile Change?

A plausible explanation is that introducing an end-to-end latent interface changes which games are easiest for the policy to optimize. All of JEDI’s six top-quantile games have shooter-style dynamics with five of them having the maximum action space, motivating the aggregate breakdown in fig. 12 (see also table 4). As summarized in fig. 12, JEDI’s largest gains are concentrated in higher-complexity games, especially games with larger action spaces and shooter-style dynamics. DIAMOND, in contrast, feeds raw image features to its actor and critic, so under a fixed compute budget it must spend capacity on both representation learning and policy/value learning. JEDI instead gives the actor and critic a learned latent zt0∈ℝ16×8×8z_{t}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{16\times 8\times 8} rather than an observation in ℝ64×64×3\mathbb{R}^{64\times 64\times 3}, making the actor-critic input about 12×\times smaller and reducing the need for those networks to solve representation learning themselves.

Intuitively, the effective interaction space between inputs and action/value prediction can grow combinatorially—often effectively exponentially—with input dimension, so this reduction may matter most in large-action, visually complex games. We regard this as an interpretation supported by the empirical pattern, not as a formal causal proof.

5.3 Qualitative Analysis

The changed task-level performance profile is also visible qualitatively (fig. 13). On BankHeist, DemonAttack, and Hero—all in JEDI’s top relative-performance quantile—JEDI learns visibly different policies from DIAMOND: it repeatedly re-enters maps in BankHeist to collect easy bank spawns while avoiding self-destructive FIRE actions, more reliably destroys obstacles in Hero, and actively tracks and neutralizes enemies in DemonAttack rather than staying in a corner and firing ineffectively.

We view these trajectories as consistent with the broader performance-profile story: moving to an end-to-end predictive latent may help more on complex games with large action spaces and shooter dynamics, where a compressed world-model latent may better align the policy-learning interface with downstream value estimation.

Conclusion

To our knowledge, JEDI is the first to show that diffusion world models can be trained in an end-to-end predictive latent space using JEPA-style learning. JEDI preseres strong online MBRL performance and substantially improving efficiency over pixel diffusion. Beyond the immediate compute gains, our results suggest that predictive latent learning changes the behavior of the world model itself: JEDI exhibits a markedly different task-level performance profile from pixel-space diffusion, indicating that end-to-end latent learning affects more than runtime and memory alone. Together with the information-bottleneck perspective developed in our theory section, these findings position predictive latent diffusion as a principled and practical direction for scaling online MBRL.

Limitations.

Our evidence is limited to Atari100k (5 seeds) and four Craftium tasks (3 seeds; figs. 4 and 5), so we have not yet tested JEDI on DMControl, Procgen, or higher-resolution domains. JEDI is also not the fastest latent method: HI trains in 27 A100-hours versus our 38, though HI uses a pretrained perceptual model and 97M parameters, versus JEDI’s 13.5M (table 1). Theoretically, eqs. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 motivate representation-learning properties rather than guaranteeing optimization. Performance also depends on several design choices, including tanh clamping and random switching (figs. 9 and 10); DIAMOND and HI also use clamping, and DIAMOND additionally uses latent discretization. Finally, performance is sensitive to denoiser batch size, so we report the better of batch sizes 32 and 64 for each task; HI similarly reports results across multiple hyperparameter settings.

6 Related Works

World models and online MBRL.

Classic approaches such as Dyna and PlaNet established predictive world models for control [59, 25]. Search-based successors such as MuZero and EfficientZero are outside our scope because we focus on online MBRL without look-ahead planning [57, 53, 70]. Dreamer and its successors showed that actor-critic learning on imagined trajectories scales to visual domains [24, 26, 27]. IRIS, TWM, STORM, and TWISTER expanded the Atari100k design space with sequence-model world models [43, 49, 73, 12]. DIAMOND introduced strong pixel diffusion for online MBRL, while Horizon Imagination moved diffusion to a separately learned latent space [3, 16]. Other concurrent methods add annotations, event supervision, or explicit exploration [72, 47, 17] and are beyond our scope of studying end-to-end latent diffusion for MBRL world model backbone.

JEPA and predictive representations.

Early work argued that representations should preserve predictive structure rather than reconstruct raw detail [52], a view further developed by modern JEPA-style methods [22, 13, 4, 8, 5]. Related predictive-latent methods also perform well in model-based control [29, 28, 41, 65]. Recent work further connects JEPA to the information bottleneck [60, 2, 56, 64, 55, 54]. To our knowledge, JEDI is the first online world model to combine a JEPA-style objective with diffusion denoising and an information-bottleneck interpretation.

Diffusion

Diffusion models are now a standard generative framework [58, 30, 34]. Many high-capacity systems use separately learned latent spaces for efficiency [50, 19, 11, 46, 37]. LSGM also studied end-to-end latent generative modeling, but with reconstruction-based training [62]. Diffusion has also been effective in planning, control, and offline world modeling [32, 15, 31, 66, 21, 39, 18], and has been used for representation learning through denoising-step search, distillation, compressed conditioning, and hidden-feature extraction [40, 71, 69, 74, 45, 44, 7, 68]. JEDI instead learns and predicts compressed latents end to end through a JEPA-style diffusion world-model objective.

Appendix A Technical appendices and supplementary material

A.1 JEPA as a Variational Information Bottleneck

We consider two observed views or two sequential observations, x1x_{1} and x2x_{2}, together with latent representations z1z_{1} and z2z_{2}. The assumed probabilistic graphical model is

x1←z1→z2→x2.x_{1}\leftarrow z_{1}\rightarrow z_{2}\rightarrow x_{2}.

Under this model, the joint distribution factorizes as

pθ​(x1,x2,z1,z2)=p⁡(z1)​pθ​(z2∣z1)​p​(x1∣z1)​p​(x2∣z2).p_{\theta}(x_{1},x_{2},z_{1},z_{2})=p(z_{1})\,p_{\theta}(z_{2}\mid z_{1})\,p(x_{1}\mid z_{1})\,p(x_{2}\mid z_{2}). (11)

Here, pθ​(z2∣z1)p_{\theta}(z_{2}\mid z_{1}) plays the role of the JEPA predictor: it predicts the latent representation of the second view from the latent representation of the first view.

We introduce the amortized variational posterior

qϕ(z1,z2∣x1,x2)=qϕ(z1∣x1)qϕ(z2∣x2).q_{\phi}(z_{1},z_{2}\mid x_{1},x_{2})=q_{\phi}(z_{1}\mid x_{1})q_{\phi}(z_{2}\mid x_{2}). (12)

For notational compactness, for a fixed pair (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}), define

q1​(z1):=qϕ​(z1∣x1),q2​(z2):=qϕ​(z2∣x2),q12​(z1,z2):=q1​(z1)​q2​(z2).q_{1}(z_{1}):=q_{\phi}(z_{1}\mid x_{1}),\qquad q_{2}(z_{2}):=q_{\phi}(z_{2}\mid x_{2}),\qquad q_{12}(z_{1},z_{2}):=q_{1}(z_{1})q_{2}(z_{2}).
Variational decomposition of the joint likelihood.

We begin with the marginal log-likelihood of the two views. Since q12q_{12} is a normalized distribution over z1,z2z_{1},z_{2}, we may write

log⁡pθ​(x1,x2)\displaystyle\log p_{\theta}(x_{1},x_{2}) =∫q12​(z1,z2)​log⁡pθ​(x1,x2)​d​z1​d​z2\displaystyle=\int q_{12}(z_{1},z_{2})\log p_{\theta}(x_{1},x_{2})\,\mathrm{d}z_{1}\mathrm{d}z_{2}
=∫q12​(z1,z2)​log⁡pθ​(x1,x2,z1,z2)pθ(z1,z2∣x1,x2)​d​z1​d​z2\displaystyle=\int q_{12}(z_{1},z_{2})\log\frac{p_{\theta}(x_{1},x_{2},z_{1},z_{2})}{p_{\theta}(z_{1},z_{2}\mid x_{1},x_{2})}\,\mathrm{d}z_{1}\mathrm{d}z_{2}
=𝔼q12[logpθ​(x1,x2,z1,z2)q12​(z1,z2)]+DKL(q12(z1,z2)∥pθ(z1,z2∣x1,x2)).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{12}}\left[\log\frac{p_{\theta}(x_{1},x_{2},z_{1},z_{2})}{q_{12}(z_{1},z_{2})}\right]+D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{12}(z_{1},z_{2})\,\middle\|\,p_{\theta}(z_{1},z_{2}\mid x_{1},x_{2})\right). (13)

Define the posterior gap

Δθ(x1,x2):=DKL(q12(z1,z2)∥pθ(z1,z2∣x1,x2)).\Delta_{\theta}(x_{1},x_{2}):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{12}(z_{1},z_{2})\,\middle\|\,p_{\theta}(z_{1},z_{2}\mid x_{1},x_{2})\right). (14)

Substituting the factorization in Eq. (11) into Eq. (13), we obtain

log⁡pθ​(x1,x2)\displaystyle\log p_{\theta}(x_{1},x_{2}) =𝔼q1​[log⁡p⁡(x1∣z1)]+𝔼q2​[log⁡p⁡(x2∣z2)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}}\left[\log p(x_{1}\mid z_{1})\right]+\mathbb{E}_{q_{2}}\left[\log p(x_{2}\mid z_{2})\right]
−𝔼q1​[DKL​(q2​(z2)∥pθ​(z2∣z1))]−DKL​(q1​(z1)∥p⁡(z1))+Δθ​(x1,x2).\displaystyle\quad-\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{2}(z_{2})\,\middle\|\,p_{\theta}(z_{2}\mid z_{1})\right)\right]-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{1}(z_{1})\,\middle\|\,p(z_{1})\right)+\Delta_{\theta}(x_{1},x_{2}). (15)

The first two terms are view-likelihood terms. The third term is the JEPA prediction term. The fourth term is a bottleneck regularizer on z1z_{1}, and the final term is the posterior approximation gap.

Connection to mutual information.

The mutual information between the two views is

I⁡(X1,X2)=𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)​[log⁡p⁡(x1,x2)−log⁡p⁡(x1)−log⁡p⁡(x2)].I(X_{1};X_{2})=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})}\left[\log p(x_{1},x_{2})-\log p(x_{1})-\log p(x_{2})\right]. (16)

Assuming the model marginal matches the population distribution, define the variational estimates

I^​(X1,Z1)\displaystyle\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1}) :=𝔼p⁡(x1)​qϕ​(z1∣x1)​[log⁡p⁡(x1∣z1)−log⁡p⁡(x1)],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1})q_{\phi}(z_{1}\mid x_{1})}\left[\log p(x_{1}\mid z_{1})-\log p(x_{1})\right], (17)
I^​(X2,Z2)\displaystyle\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2}) :=𝔼p⁡(x2)​qϕ​(z2∣x2)​[log⁡p⁡(x2∣z2)−log⁡p⁡(x2)].\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{2})q_{\phi}(z_{2}\mid x_{2})}\left[\log p(x_{2}\mid z_{2})-\log p(x_{2})\right]. (18)

Now define the JEPA prediction loss

ℒJEPA:=𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)​qϕ​(z1∣x1)​[DKL​(qϕ​(z2∣x2)∥pθ​(z2∣z1))],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})q_{\phi}(z_{1}\mid x_{1})}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{\phi}(z_{2}\mid x_{2})\,\middle\|\,p_{\theta}(z_{2}\mid z_{1})\right)\right], (19)

the bottleneck regularizer

ℛ1:=𝔼p⁡(x1)​[DKL​(qϕ​(z1∣x1)∥p⁡(z1))],\mathcal{R}_{1}:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1})}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{\phi}(z_{1}\mid x_{1})\,\middle\|\,p(z_{1})\right)\right], (20)

and the expected posterior gap

𝒢:=𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)[DKL(qϕ(z1,z2∣x1,x2)∥pθ(z1,z2∣x1,x2))].\mathcal{G}:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{\phi}(z_{1},z_{2}\mid x_{1},x_{2})\,\middle\|\,p_{\theta}(z_{1},z_{2}\mid x_{1},x_{2})\right)\right]. (21)

Then

I⁡(X1,X2)=I^​(X1,Z1)+I^​(X2,Z2)−ℒJEPA−ℛ1+𝒢.I(X_{1};X_{2})=\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1})+\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}-\mathcal{R}_{1}+\mathcal{G}. (22)

Equivalently,

−ℒJEPA=I⁡(X1,X2)−I^​(X1,Z1)−I^​(X2,Z2)+ℛ1−𝒢.-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}=I(X_{1};X_{2})-\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1})-\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2})+\mathcal{R}_{1}-\mathcal{G}. (23)

Under the generative Markov chain X1−Z1−Z2−X2X_{1}-Z_{1}-Z_{2}-X_{2}, the data processing inequality gives

I⁡(X1,X2)≤I⁡(Z1,Z2),I(X_{1};X_{2})\leq I(Z_{1};Z_{2}), (24)

and therefore

−ℒJEPA≤I⁡(Z1,Z2)−I^​(X1,Z1)−I^​(X2,Z2)+ℛ1−𝒢.-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}\leq I(Z_{1};Z_{2})-\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1})-\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2})+\mathcal{R}_{1}-\mathcal{G}. (25)

A.2 Conditional Diffusion-JEPA as a Variational Information Bottleneck

We now extend the variational JEPA argument to a latent conditional diffusion predictor. The key difference from the one-step JEPA model is that the direct predictor pθ​(z2∣z1)p_{\theta}(z_{2}\mid z_{1}) is replaced by a conditional reverse diffusion trajectory that predicts the clean target latent z20z_{2}^{0} from noise while conditioning on the clean context latent z10z_{1}^{0}.

We consider two observed views x1x_{1} and x2x_{2}. The clean context latent is z10z_{1}^{0}, and the target latent is represented by a diffusion path

z20:T:=(z20,z21,…,z2T),z_{2}^{0:T}:=(z_{2}^{0},z_{2}^{1},\ldots,z_{2}^{T}),

where z20z_{2}^{0} is the clean target latent and z2Tz_{2}^{T} is the maximally noised latent. The assumed graphical model is shown in fig. 3, where each reverse denoising transition is conditioned on z10z_{1}^{0}. Equivalently, the joint distribution factorizes as

pψ(x1,x2,z10,z20:T)\displaystyle p_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2},z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T}) =p⁡(z10)​p​(x1∣z10)​p​(z2T)​∏t=1Tpψ​(z2t−1∣z2t,z10)​p​(x2∣z20).\displaystyle=p(z_{1}^{0})\,p(x_{1}\mid z_{1}^{0})\,p(z_{2}^{T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})\,p(x_{2}\mid z_{2}^{0}). (26)

Here,

pψ(z20:T∣z10):=p(z2T)∏t=1Tpψ(z2t−1∣z2t,z10)p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{0:T}\mid z_{1}^{0}):=p(z_{2}^{T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})

is the conditional reverse diffusion path. Therefore, the induced stochastic JEPA predictor from z10z_{1}^{0} to z20z_{2}^{0} is

pψ(z20∣z10)=∫p(z2T)∏t=1Tpψ(z2t−1∣z2t,z10)dz21:T.p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid z_{1}^{0})=\int p(z_{2}^{T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})\,\mathrm{d}z_{2}^{1:T}. (27)

Thus, the conditional diffusion model is a multi-step stochastic JEPA predictor.

We introduce the amortized variational posterior

qφ(z10,z20:T∣x1,x2)\displaystyle q_{\varphi}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T}\mid x_{1},x_{2}) =qφ(z10∣x1)qφ(z20∣x2)q(z21:T∣z20),\displaystyle=q_{\varphi}(z_{1}^{0}\mid x_{1})\,q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})\,q(z_{2}^{1:T}\mid z_{2}^{0}), (28)

where q(z21:T∣z20)q(z_{2}^{1:T}\mid z_{2}^{0}) is the fixed forward diffusion process. For notational compactness, for a fixed pair (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}), define

q1​(z10):=qφ​(z10∣x1),q_{1}(z_{1}^{0}):=q_{\varphi}(z_{1}^{0}\mid x_{1}),
q20​(z20):=qφ​(z20∣x2),q_{2}^{0}(z_{2}^{0}):=q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2}),
q20:T(z20:T):=q20(z20)q(z21:T∣z20),q_{2}^{0:T}(z_{2}^{0:T}):=q_{2}^{0}(z_{2}^{0})q(z_{2}^{1:T}\mid z_{2}^{0}),

and

q12(z10,z20:T):=q1(z10)q20:T(z20:T).q_{12}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T}):=q_{1}(z_{1}^{0})q_{2}^{0:T}(z_{2}^{0:T}).
Variational decomposition of the joint likelihood.

We begin with the marginal log-likelihood of the two views. Since q12q_{12} is a normalized distribution over z10,z20:Tz_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T}, we may write

log⁡pψ​(x1,x2)\displaystyle\log p_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2}) =∫q12(z10,z20:T)logpψ(x1,x2)dz10dz20:T\displaystyle=\int q_{12}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T})\log p_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2})\,\mathrm{d}z_{1}^{0}\mathrm{d}z_{2}^{0:T}
=∫q12(z10,z20:T)logpψ(x1,x2,z10,z20:T)pψ(z10,z20:T∣x1,x2)dz10dz20:T\displaystyle=\int q_{12}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T})\log\frac{p_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2},z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T})}{p_{\psi}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T}\mid x_{1},x_{2})}\,\mathrm{d}z_{1}^{0}\mathrm{d}z_{2}^{0:T}
=𝔼q12[logpψ(x1,x2,z10,z20:T)q12(z10,z20:T)]+DKL(q12(z10,z20:T)∥pψ(z10,z20:T∣x1,x2)).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{12}}\left[\log\frac{p_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2},z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T})}{q_{12}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T})}\right]+D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{12}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T})\,\middle\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T}\mid x_{1},x_{2})\right). (29)

Define the posterior gap

Δψ(x1,x2):=DKL(q12(z10,z20:T)∥pψ(z10,z20:T∣x1,x2)).\Delta_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2}):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{12}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T})\,\middle\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T}\mid x_{1},x_{2})\right). (30)

Substituting the factorization in Eq. (26) into Eq. (29), we obtain

log⁡pψ​(x1,x2)\displaystyle\log p_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2}) =𝔼q12[logp(x1∣z10)+logp(x2∣z20)+logp(z10)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{12}}\Bigg[\log p(x_{1}\mid z_{1}^{0})+\log p(x_{2}\mid z_{2}^{0})+\log p(z_{1}^{0})
+logp(z2T)+∑t=1Tlogpψ(z2t−1∣z2t,z10)−logq1(z10)−logq20:T(z20:T)]\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\log p(z_{2}^{T})+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})-\log q_{1}(z_{1}^{0})-\log q_{2}^{0:T}(z_{2}^{0:T})\Bigg]
+Δψ​(x1,x2).\displaystyle\quad+\Delta_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2}). (31)

Now group the terms according to their roles. The view-likelihood terms are

𝔼q12​[log⁡p⁡(x1∣z10)]=𝔼q1​[log⁡p⁡(x1∣z10)]\mathbb{E}_{q_{12}}[\log p(x_{1}\mid z_{1}^{0})]=\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}}[\log p(x_{1}\mid z_{1}^{0})]

and

𝔼q12​[log⁡p⁡(x2∣z20)]=𝔼q20​[log⁡p⁡(x2∣z20)].\mathbb{E}_{q_{12}}[\log p(x_{2}\mid z_{2}^{0})]=\mathbb{E}_{q_{2}^{0}}[\log p(x_{2}\mid z_{2}^{0})].

The context-prior terms satisfy

𝔼q12​[log⁡p⁡(z10)−log⁡q1​(z10)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q_{12}}\left[\log p(z_{1}^{0})-\log q_{1}(z_{1}^{0})\right] =−DKL​(q1​(z10)∥p⁡(z10)).\displaystyle=-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{1}(z_{1}^{0})\,\middle\|\,p(z_{1}^{0})\right). (32)

The target-path terms satisfy

𝔼q12[logp(z2T)+∑t=1Tlogpψ(z2t−1∣z2t,z10)−logq20:T(z20:T)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q_{12}}\left[\log p(z_{2}^{T})+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})-\log q_{2}^{0:T}(z_{2}^{0:T})\right]
=−𝔼q1[DKL(q20:T(z20:T)∥pψ(z20:T∣z10))].\displaystyle\qquad=-\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{2}^{0:T}(z_{2}^{0:T})\,\middle\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{0:T}\mid z_{1}^{0})\right)\right]. (33)

Therefore,

log⁡pψ​(x1,x2)\displaystyle\log p_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2}) =𝔼q1​[log⁡p⁡(x1∣z10)]+𝔼q20​[log⁡p⁡(x2∣z20)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}}\left[\log p(x_{1}\mid z_{1}^{0})\right]+\mathbb{E}_{q_{2}^{0}}\left[\log p(x_{2}\mid z_{2}^{0})\right]
−𝔼q1[DKL(q20:T(z20:T)∥pψ(z20:T∣z10))]\displaystyle\quad-\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{2}^{0:T}(z_{2}^{0:T})\,\middle\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{0:T}\mid z_{1}^{0})\right)\right]
−DKL​(q1​(z10)∥p⁡(z10))+Δψ​(x1,x2).\displaystyle\quad-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{1}(z_{1}^{0})\,\middle\|\,p(z_{1}^{0})\right)+\Delta_{\psi}(x_{1},x_{2}). (34)

The first two terms are view-likelihood terms. The third term is the conditional diffusion-JEPA prediction term. The fourth term is a bottleneck regularizer on the clean context latent z10z_{1}^{0}, and the final term is the posterior approximation gap.

Define the instance-level conditional diffusion path loss

ℒCDJpath(x1,x2):=𝔼q1[DKL(q20:T(z20:T)∥pψ(z20:T∣z10))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}(x_{1},x_{2}):=\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{2}^{0:T}(z_{2}^{0:T})\,\middle\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{0:T}\mid z_{1}^{0})\right)\right]. (35)

This is the direct analogue of the one-step JEPA prediction loss 𝔼q1[DKL(q2(z2)∥pθ(z2∣z1))]\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{2}(z_{2})\|p_{\theta}(z_{2}\mid z_{1}))], except that the predicted object is now the entire reverse diffusion path z20:Tz_{2}^{0:T}.

To see the diffusion terms explicitly, write

ℒCDJpath​(x1,x2)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}(x_{1},x_{2}) =𝔼q1q20:T[logq20:T(z20:T)−logp(z2T)−∑t=1Tlogpψ(z2t−1∣z2t,z10)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}q_{2}^{0:T}}\Bigg[\log q_{2}^{0:T}(z_{2}^{0:T})-\log p(z_{2}^{T})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})\Bigg]. (36)

Since

q20:T(z20:T)=q20(z20)q(z21:T∣z20),q_{2}^{0:T}(z_{2}^{0:T})=q_{2}^{0}(z_{2}^{0})q(z_{2}^{1:T}\mid z_{2}^{0}),

we may also write

ℒCDJpath​(x1,x2)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}(x_{1},x_{2}) =𝔼q1q20q(z21:T∣z20)[logq20(z20)+logq(z21:T∣z20)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}q_{2}^{0}q(z_{2}^{1:T}\mid z_{2}^{0})}\Bigg[\log q_{2}^{0}(z_{2}^{0})+\log q(z_{2}^{1:T}\mid z_{2}^{0})
−logp(z2T)−∑t=1Tlogpψ(z2t−1∣z2t,z10)].\displaystyle\qquad\qquad-\log p(z_{2}^{T})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})\Bigg]. (37)

For a Markov forward diffusion process, this path loss admits the usual DDPM decomposition. Using

q(z21:T∣z20)=q(z2T∣z20)∏t=2Tq(z2t−1∣z2t,z20),q(z_{2}^{1:T}\mid z_{2}^{0})=q(z_{2}^{T}\mid z_{2}^{0})\prod_{t=2}^{T}q(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{2}^{0}),

we obtain

ℒCDJpath​(x1,x2)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}(x_{1},x_{2}) =−H⁡(q20)+𝔼q20​[DKL​(q⁡(z2T∣z20)∥p⁡(z2T))]\displaystyle=-H(q_{2}^{0})+\mathbb{E}_{q_{2}^{0}}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q(z_{2}^{T}\mid z_{2}^{0})\,\middle\|\,p(z_{2}^{T})\right)\right]
+𝔼q1​q20​q​(z21∣z20)​[−log⁡pψ​(z20∣z21,z10)]\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}q_{2}^{0}q(z_{2}^{1}\mid z_{2}^{0})}\left[-\log p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid z_{2}^{1},z_{1}^{0})\right]
+∑t=2T𝔼q1​q20​q​(z2t∣z20)[DKL(q(z2t−1∣z2t,z20)∥pψ(z2t−1∣z2t,z10))].\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{t=2}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}q_{2}^{0}q(z_{2}^{t}\mid z_{2}^{0})}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{2}^{0})\,\middle\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})\right)\right]. (38)

The first term is the entropy of the target encoder distribution, the second term is the terminal prior-matching term, the third term is the endpoint reconstruction term for z20z_{2}^{0}, and the remaining terms are the conditional denoising KLs.

Connection to mutual information.

The mutual information between the two views is

I⁡(X1,X2)=𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)​[log⁡p⁡(x1,x2)−log⁡p⁡(x1)−log⁡p⁡(x2)].I(X_{1};X_{2})=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})}\left[\log p(x_{1},x_{2})-\log p(x_{1})-\log p(x_{2})\right]. (39)

Assuming the model marginal matches the population distribution, define the variational estimates

I^​(X1,Z10)\displaystyle\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1}^{0}) :=𝔼p⁡(x1)​qφ​(z10∣x1)​[log⁡p⁡(x1∣z10)−log⁡p⁡(x1)],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1})q_{\varphi}(z_{1}^{0}\mid x_{1})}\left[\log p(x_{1}\mid z_{1}^{0})-\log p(x_{1})\right], (40)
I^​(X2,Z20)\displaystyle\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2}^{0}) :=𝔼p⁡(x2)​qφ​(z20∣x2)​[log⁡p⁡(x2∣z20)−log⁡p⁡(x2)].\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{2})q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})}\left[\log p(x_{2}\mid z_{2}^{0})-\log p(x_{2})\right]. (41)

Now define the population-level conditional diffusion-JEPA path loss

ℒCDJpath:=𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)​[ℒCDJpath​(x1,x2)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}(x_{1},x_{2})\right], (42)

the bottleneck regularizer

ℛ1:=𝔼p⁡(x1)​[DKL​(qφ​(z10∣x1)∥p⁡(z10))],\mathcal{R}_{1}:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1})}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{\varphi}(z_{1}^{0}\mid x_{1})\,\middle\|\,p(z_{1}^{0})\right)\right], (43)

and the expected posterior gap

𝒢:=𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)[DKL(qφ(z10,z20:T∣x1,x2)∥pψ(z10,z20:T∣x1,x2))].\mathcal{G}:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{\varphi}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T}\mid x_{1},x_{2})\,\middle\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{1}^{0},z_{2}^{0:T}\mid x_{1},x_{2})\right)\right]. (44)

Taking the expectation of Eq. (34) over p⁡(x1,x2)p(x_{1},x_{2}) and subtracting log⁡p⁡(x1)+log⁡p⁡(x2)\log p(x_{1})+\log p(x_{2}) gives

I⁡(X1,X2)=I^​(X1,Z10)+I^​(X2,Z20)−ℒCDJpath−ℛ1+𝒢.I(X_{1};X_{2})=\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1}^{0})+\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2}^{0})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}-\mathcal{R}_{1}+\mathcal{G}. (45)

Equivalently,

−ℒCDJpath=I⁡(X1,X2)−I^​(X1,Z10)−I^​(X2,Z20)+ℛ1−𝒢.-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}=I(X_{1};X_{2})-\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1}^{0})-\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2}^{0})+\mathcal{R}_{1}-\mathcal{G}. (46)

After marginalizing the intermediate diffusion variables z21:Tz_{2}^{1:T}, the model induces the clean-latent Markov structure

X1−Z10−Z20−X2.X_{1}-Z_{1}^{0}-Z_{2}^{0}-X_{2}.

Therefore, by the data processing inequality,

I⁡(X1,X2)≤I⁡(Z10,Z20).I(X_{1};X_{2})\leq I(Z_{1}^{0};Z_{2}^{0}). (47)

Substituting this into Eq. (46) gives

−ℒCDJpath≤I⁡(Z10,Z20)−I^​(X1,Z10)−I^​(X2,Z20)+ℛ1−𝒢.-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}\leq I(Z_{1}^{0};Z_{2}^{0})-\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1}^{0})-\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2}^{0})+\mathcal{R}_{1}-\mathcal{G}. (48)

Finally, if one optimizes only the DDPM-style learnable denoising part of the path objective, define

ℒ0\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{0} :=𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)​𝔼q1​q20​q​(z21∣z20)​[−log⁡pψ​(z20∣z21,z10)],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})}\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}q_{2}^{0}q(z_{2}^{1}\mid z_{2}^{0})}\left[-\log p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid z_{2}^{1},z_{1}^{0})\right],
ℒCDJden\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{den}} :=ℒ0+𝔼p⁡(x1,x2)​∑t=2T𝔼q1​q20​q​(z2t∣z20)​[DKL​(q⁡(z2t−1∣z2t,z20)∥pψ​(z2t−1∣z2t,z10))].\displaystyle:=\mathcal{L}^{0}+\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1},x_{2})}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{q_{1}q_{2}^{0}q(z_{2}^{t}\mid z_{2}^{0})}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{2}^{0})\,\middle\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{2}^{t-1}\mid z_{2}^{t},z_{1}^{0})\right)\right]. (49)

Then

ℒCDJpath=𝒞2+ℛ2,T+ℒCDJden,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}=\mathcal{C}_{2}+\mathcal{R}_{2,T}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{den}}, (50)

where

ℛ2,T:=𝔼p⁡(x2)​qφ​(z20∣x2)​[DKL​(q⁡(z2T∣z20)∥p⁡(z2T))]\mathcal{R}_{2,T}:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{2})q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q(z_{2}^{T}\mid z_{2}^{0})\,\middle\|\,p(z_{2}^{T})\right)\right] (51)

is the terminal prior-matching term, while

𝒞2:=𝔼p⁡(x2)​[−H⁡(qφ​(z20∣x2))]=𝔼p⁡(x2)​qφ​(z20∣x2)​[log⁡qφ​(z20∣x2)]\mathcal{C}_{2}:=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{2})}\left[-H\bigl(q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})\bigr)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{2})q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})}\left[\log q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})\right] (52)

is the ψ\psi-independent remainder. Substituting Eq. (50) into Eq. (48) yields

−ℒCDJden\displaystyle-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{den}} ≤I⁡(Z10,Z20)−I^​(X1,Z10)−I^​(X2,Z20)\displaystyle\leq I(Z_{1}^{0};Z_{2}^{0})-\widehat{I}(X_{1};Z_{1}^{0})-\widehat{I}(X_{2};Z_{2}^{0})
+ℛ1+ℛ2,T−𝒢+𝒞2.\displaystyle\quad+\mathcal{R}_{1}+\mathcal{R}_{2,T}-\mathcal{G}+\mathcal{C}_{2}. (53)

Therefore, even when training is written only as a conditional denoising objective, the conditional diffusion-JEPA loss exhibits the same variational information-bottleneck structure as the one-step JEPA loss, up to terminal diffusion regularization, endpoint constants, and the variational posterior gap.

A.2.1 Remark on optimizing the bottleneck regularizer.

The decomposition above shows that the exact variational information-bottleneck objective is

minφ,ψ⁡ℒCDJpath+ℛ1,\min_{\varphi,\psi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}+\mathcal{R}_{1}, (54)

or, more generally,

minφ,ψ⁡ℒCDJpath+β​ℛ1.\min_{\varphi,\psi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}+\beta\mathcal{R}_{1}. (55)

In our experiments, we do not directly optimize the exact KL regularizer ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}. Accordingly, the most precise interpretation of JEDI is that it optimizes the conditional diffusion prediction term that appears inside the variational information-bottleneck decomposition, rather than exactly optimizing the full variational information-bottleneck objective. We therefore present the bottleneck view as a theoretical justification and design lens for the current method, while treating explicit optimization of ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} as a promising extension.

Relation to VICReg and LeJEPA [6, 55]

The bottleneck regularizer ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} also clarifies the connection between our variational view and recent explicit regularization methods for collapse-free joint embedding learning. We do not incorporate such regularizers here, since our empirical study focuses on conventional JEPA training, but the decomposition reveals a close conceptual link.

By the standard decomposition,

ℛ1=𝔼p⁡(x1)​DKL​(qφ​(z10∣x1)∥p⁡(z10))=Iq​(X1,Z10)+DKL​(qφ​(z10)∥p⁡(z10)).\mathcal{R}_{1}=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{1})}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{\varphi}(z_{1}^{0}\mid x_{1})\,\middle\|\,p(z_{1}^{0})\right)=I_{q}(X_{1};Z_{1}^{0})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{\varphi}(z_{1}^{0})\,\middle\|\,p(z_{1}^{0})\right). (56)

The first term is the information-bottleneck component, which explicitly penalizes the information retained by the context representation. The second term is an aggregate distribution-matching regularizer. When p⁡(z10)=𝒩⁡(0,I)p(z_{1}^{0})=\mathcal{N}(0,I), this aggregate term encourages the representation distribution to be centered, non-collapsed, and isotropic. This is closely related in spirit to the variance and covariance regularizers used in VICReg, which maintain per-dimension variance and decorrelate embedding coordinates, and to the SIGReg regularizer used in LeJEPA, which directly encourages embeddings to match an isotropic Gaussian distribution.

Thus, ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} can be viewed as a variational counterpart to these explicit representation regularizers, with an additional information-bottleneck interpretation.

A.2.2 Remark on 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} remainder term

With the exact DDPM KL decomposition, the remainder term has the explicit form

𝒞2​(x2):=−H⁡(qφ​(z20∣x2))=𝔼qφ​(z20∣x2)​[log⁡qφ​(z20∣x2)].\mathcal{C}_{2}(x_{2}):=-H(q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2}))=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})}\left[\log q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})\right]. (57)

At the population level,

𝒞2=𝔼p⁡(x2)​[𝔼qφ​(z20∣x2)​log⁡qφ​(z20∣x2)].\mathcal{C}_{2}=\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{2})}\left[\mathbb{E}_{q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})}\log q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2})\right]. (58)

Thus,

ℒCDJpath=𝒞2+ℛ2,T+ℒCDJden.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{path}}=\mathcal{C}_{2}+\mathcal{R}_{2,T}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDJ}}^{\mathrm{den}}. (59)

When qφ​(z20∣x2)q_{\varphi}(z_{2}^{0}\mid x_{2}) has fixed entropy, for example under a deterministic or fixed-variance target encoder with stop-gradient, 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} is constant with respect to the conditional reverse parameters ψ\psi. If the target encoder distribution is learnable through this objective, however, 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} may depend on φ\varphi and should not be treated as a global constant.

A.3 JEDI Algorithm

Green font refers to changes as compared to pixel-based diffusion world model baseline [3]

Appendix B Changes Compared to Baseline and Hyperparameters

We used the DIAMOND library [3] (MIT License) for our implementation. The main difference between JEDI World Model and DIAMOND is the transplant of the DIAMOND’s RL encoder onto the JEDI World Model and the techniques implemented to facilitate end-to-end latent diffusion mentioned in section 3. The only network architectural changes are practical: (1) changing the original RL encoder to downsample to zt∈[−3,3]16×8×8z_{t}\in[-3,3]^{16\times 8\times 8}, (2) modifying the diffusion UNET [51] into a single layer without downsampling, (3) and removing the downsampling in the Reward/Termination Model’s encoder. The only hyperparameter changes were increasing the diffusion model’s warm-up learning steps to 1000 and sigma of input data to be 1.

B.1 Benchmark and environment settings

Atari100k.

We follow the standard Atari100k protocol used by prior online world-model work and the IRIS evaluation codebase. In particular, each run uses the 26-game Atari100k benchmark with a total budget of 100100k environment interactions, and we report results over 5 seeds per task as described in section 4.1. Observations are RGB frames resized to 64×6464\times 64, matching the image interface used by the JEDI encoder and world model. We use the standard Atari v4 setup with frame skip 4, which matches the protocol used in prior Atari100k world-model evaluations.

Evaluation metrics.

Following Agarwal et al. [1], we compute aggregate Atari100k metrics from human-normalized scores (HNS). For a game with agent score SagentS_{\mathrm{agent}}, random-policy score SrandomS_{\mathrm{random}}, and human score ShumanS_{\mathrm{human}}, the human-normalized score is

HNS=Sagent−SrandomShuman−Srandom.\mathrm{HNS}=\frac{S_{\mathrm{agent}}-S_{\mathrm{random}}}{S_{\mathrm{human}}-S_{\mathrm{random}}}.

An HNS of 11 corresponds to human-level performance. “Mean” refers to the arithmetic mean of HNS values across the benchmark. “IQM” (interquartile mean) is the mean of the middle 50% of HNS values across game seed runs, which makes it more robust to outliers than the plain mean. “Optimality Gap” measures how far performance remains below human level, and is reported as the average gap to the threshold HNS=1\mathrm{HNS}=1, i.e., 𝔼⁡[max⁡(1−HNS,0)]\mathbb{E}[\max(1-\mathrm{HNS},0)], so lower is better.

Craftium.

For Craftium, we evaluate on four tasks with 3 seeds per task, as described in section 4.1. We use standard visual observations with RGB images resized to 64×6464\times 64, so that the same encoder and latent world-model interface used on Atari can be applied directly in the 3D setting. We use 300 training steps and 200 collection steps per epoch. We report the training returns. We leverage the symlog reward prediction used in HI [16] for the continuous reward task, Speleo. We also follow HI and use 30k environment steps for SmallRoom-v0 and 100k environment steps for the other 3 environments
